props.title: Requiem for a Dream
props.initialSlug: Addiction spirals destroy four lives in Brooklyn

sections.content: Requiem for a Dream (2000) stands as one of cinema's most visceral portrayals of addiction. Director Darren Aronofsky crafts a relentless descent into psychological horror through four interconnected characters, using rapid-fire montages, split-screen techniques, and Clint Mansell's haunting score "Lux Aeterna." The film builds on the experimental techniques Aronofsky developed in Pi (1998), but amplifies them to create a uniquely harrowing viewing experience. Ellen Burstyn's Oscar-nominated performance as Sara Goldfarb remains one of the most devastating portraits of isolation and desperation ever captured on screen.

sections.content: The film's innovative editing techniques influenced a generation of filmmakers. The repeated "hip-hop montages" showing drug use became a frequently imitated style, seen later in films like Traffic (2000) and 21 Grams (2003). Aronofsky's use of extreme close-ups and distorted lenses to convey psychological deterioration created a new visual language for depicting addiction and mental illness on screen. The film's unflinching approach paved the way for later works like Beautiful Boy (2018) and Euphoria (2019-present).

What sets Requiem for a Dream apart is how it portrays addiction beyond just illegal drugs. Sara's descent through diet pills and television addiction speaks to broader societal issues of isolation and the American dream. This multi-layered examination of compulsive behavior influenced later films like Shame (2011) and Thanks for Sharing (2012), which explored different forms of addiction through a similar psychological lens. sections.content: The film's technical achievements remain groundbreaking. Matthew Libatique's cinematography alternates between handheld intimacy and precisely choreographed sequences that mirror the characters' loss of control. The famous "split-screen" sequences influenced later films like 127 Hours (2010) and Maniac (2012). The combination of Snorricam shots (camera mounted directly to actors) and extreme wide-angle lenses created a disorienting effect that's been copied countless times but rarely matched in impact.
